clinical_knowledge.topic: Renal Cell Carcinoma evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Renal Cell Carcinoma is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Visible hematuria requires urgent malignancy evaluation, including renal function assessment, upper-tract imaging selected with attention to contrast safety, and cystoscopy; treatment follows confirmed staging and nephron-sparing feasibility.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: painless gross hematuria, flank pain, and palpable mass

Key HPI features: A 50-year-old female presents to the clinic with painless gross hematuria, flank pain, and palpable mass. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Renal Cell Carcinoma.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Renal Cell Carcinoma.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing painless gross hematuria exclusively to urinary tract infection without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring concerning features such as painless gross hematuria or a palpable flank mass.
management_principles: Assess hemodynamic status, anemia, renal function, and urinary retention; arrange urgent urology evaluation, appropriate upper-tract imaging, and cystoscopy, with surgery planned only after diagnosis and staging.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of painless gross hematuria, flank pain, and palpable mass. HPI: renal cell carcinoma.
reference_soap.objective: Check vital signs, abdominal/flank examination, urinalysis and culture when infection is suspected, CBC, creatinine/eGFR, and clot retention. Obtain appropriate upper-tract imaging after considering renal function and contrast risk.
reference_soap.assessment: Gross hematuria with flank pain and palpable mass is concerning for renal malignancy, but urothelial cancer and other causes remain possible.
reference_soap.plan: Arrange urgent urology assessment for cystoscopy and upper-tract imaging. Escalate immediately for hemodynamic instability, symptomatic anemia, or clot retention; plan oncologic surgery only after imaging, diagnosis, and staging.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Renal Cell Carcinoma
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Renal Cell Carcinoma
Urgently evaluate gross hematuria with renal-function-aware imaging and cystoscopy before staging-directed treatment

teaching.one_liner: Renal malignancy that may present with painless gross hematuria, flank pain, and a palpable mass.
red_flags: Gross hematuria with hemodynamic instability or clot retention
Unexplained weight loss or systemic symptoms suggesting advanced malignancy

must_ask.say: When did you first notice blood in your urine, and has it been visible throughout urination?
Have you had persistent pain in your side or noticed any swelling or lump there?
Have you had unexplained weight loss, fevers, night sweats, or persistent fatigue?
Have you ever smoked, had long-term kidney disease, or had a family history of kidney cancer?
Are you having trouble passing urine, passing clots, or feeling unable to empty your bladder?
